title: The corrupting power of workplace ‘power’
author: Ghassan Karian
summary: Ghassan Karian takes on the comforting idea that power corrupts decent people and argues that the evidence is more unsettling: power amplifies tendencies that were already there while removing the social brakes that restrained them. He draws on Dacher Keltner's Power Paradox, in which the empathy and social intelligence that win leaders their positions are the very qualities power erodes. He adds Sukhwinder Obhi's neuroscience findings that power impairs the mirroring process underlying empathy, so leaders become worse at reading others and less aware of it. He then names three structural accelerants: unchallenged authority, information asymmetry and the sycophantic board, citing Enron and the Boeing 737 Max. His case is that coaching and values programmes treat symptoms while leaving these structures intact. He closes by recommending structural remedies such as anonymised upward feedback, genuinely independent boards and formal dissent protocols.
points: Power does not corrupt so much as reveal, because it amplifies pre-existing tendencies while dismantling the social brakes that kept them in check.
Neuroscience research suggests leaders become literally less able to take the perspective of those they lead, and less likely to know it, which makes self-assessment an unreliable safeguard.
Unchallenged authority, filtered information and a compliant board are the structural accelerants that turn this tendency into organisational failure, as at Enron and Boeing.

Individual fixes like empathy workshops revert quickly, whereas structural interventions such as anonymised peer feedback, independent boards and mandatory dissent protocols make accountability the default.
quotes: Power doesn’t change people into someone they weren’t. It amplifies the pre-existing tendencies that were already there, while dismantling the social brakes that kept them in check.

The people at the top of organisations, Obhi’s research suggested, are literally less able (at a neurological level)to take the perspective of the people they lead. They become less accurate at reading emotions from faces.
When we feel powerful, the empathy regions of the brain disengage. We suddenly become more impulsive, more likely to behave inappropriately, and we generally lose touch with other people.

When leaders are not routinely exposed to honest challenge (when the boardroom dynamics have been arranged, consciously or not, to produce deference rather than debate) the empathy deficit goes unnoticed and uncorrected.

By the time a difficult truth reaches the CEO’s desk, it has often been softened, contextualised, or quietly omitted. The leader’s picture of reality becomes progressively more flattering and progressively less accurate.
But they address the symptoms at the individual level while leaving the structural accelerants entirely intact.

The organisations that manage power most effectively are not the ones that trust their leaders’ character. They are the ones that build systems that make good behaviour the path of least resistance, and accountability the default rather than the exception.
